title: Derelict Soviet Spacecraft? Dark Comet? What the Heck is 1998 KY26? - Nautilus

text:

What the Heck is 1998 KY26?It’s behavior defies explanationJCBy Jake Currie4:00 PM CST on November 16, 2026Add Nautilus to GoogleAn artist’s impression of Japan’s Hayabusa2 space mission touching down on the surface of the asteroid 1998 KY26. New observations with ESO’s Very Large Telescope (VLT)  have revealed that 1998 KY26 is just 11 m wide, almost three times smaller than previously thought, and is spinning once every 5 minutes, which is much faster than expected. The image above shows an updated size comparison between the asteroid and spacecraft.  
Hayabusa-2 is currently careening toward a rendezvous with the unknown. Launched in 2014, the Japanese spacecraft embarked on a mission to retrieve samples from asteroids and return them to Earth. It performed its duties admirably in 2018, spending a year and a half surveying the “rubble pile” asteroid Ryugu before swinging by its home planet to drop off the goods. Inside the sample return canister were traces of organic compounds from the dawn of the solar system. Now its mission has been extended until at least 2031, when it should reach its next target: the smaller, speedier, more mysterious 1998 KY26. This peculiar celestial object has puzzled astronomers since its discovery nearly 30 years ago. It’s relatively tiny—not much bigger than Hayabusa-2 itself and roughly 1/100th the diameter of Ryugu—and it rotates at a brisk clip of once every 5.35 minutes.Read more: “Nine Rebel Astronomy Theories That Went Dark”Subscribe to skip adsAdvertisement
